title: Japan's Influence on the West
objective: After this level you can explain how Japanese prints inspired the Impressionists.
summary: After Japan reopened to trade in the 1850s, its prints reached Europe. Japonisme taught Monet, Degas and Van Gogh flat color, asymmetry and bold framing.

cards.headline: In the 1850s, Japanese pictures started arriving in Europe.
cards.body: Japan had been closed to the West since about 1600. When trade resumed, prints like Level 71's reached Europe. Artists there had never seen anything quite like them.

cards.headline: A craze gets a name: Japonisme
cards.body: By the early 1870s the craze for Japanese art and design that swept France had a name, Japonisme, generally said to be coined by the critic Philippe Burty. What caught artists' eyes? Flat areas of bright color. Bold, stylized shapes. Everyday subjects. And compositions that ignored European habits: asymmetrical, off-center, framed in unexpected ways.
cards.callout: Flat color · bold shapes · everyday life · off-center framing

cards.fact: Monet lived surrounded by Japanese prints.
cards.context: At his house in Giverny he hung more than 200 of them, by Hokusai, Hiroshige, Utamaro and others. Outside, the bridge over his water garden recalls the Japanese bridges often shown in those prints. When you picture Monet's garden, you're partly picturing Japan.

mascot.line: Imagine eating breakfast every day under a wall of Hokusais. No wonder it rubbed off.
